metadata.method_name: Bench route test of prompt bans (CRN KV-splice arms, one-shot veto, prefill) in Qwen3-8B
metadata.decoding: T=1.0, top-p 1.0, no top-k, max 1024 new tokens, CRN inverse-CDF sampling
metadata.hardware: 1 x NVIDIA L4 23 GB, 6 CPUs, 66 GB RAM
metadata.baselines: arm a (full ban) and arm b (token-length-matched neutral twin) in the same pipeline with the same uniforms; placebo splice and knockout-mechanics controls

demo_subset.description: route_arms examples of the 5 gated bench tasks x 5 templates x CRN slots k=0..3 (first 4 of 20 slots per template, not hand-picked); per-arm token ids, generated text and stage joined from data/samples.jsonl

catalogue.mechanism: sort the whole list (sorted/list.sort or a hand-written full sort) and index position k-1
keep a heap bounded by k elements while scanning (or heapq.nsmallest/nlargest) and read its top
heapify all n values into one heap, then pop k times
partition around a pivot and recurse or loop into only the side that contains rank k
quickselect whose pivot is the median of the medians of groups of five, giving a worst-case linear selection
count occurrences of every value over the value range and walk the counts until k are covered

T03.spec_text:
Task: write a Python function solve(nums, k) that returns the k-th smallest value in nums. The argument nums is a list of integers with 1 <= len(nums) <= 2000, and every value lies between -10000 and 10000 inclusive; values may repeat. The argument k is an integer with 1 <= k <= len(nums), counted from 1, so k = 1 asks for the minimum and k = len(nums) for the maximum. Repeated values are counted separately: for nums = [3, 1, 3] and k = 3 the answer is 3.

Use only the Python standard library. Return only one ```python code block containing the function solve and any helpers, with no example usage and no explanation.

catalogue.mechanism: try every start position and compare the needle character by character (or by slicing) against the window
precompute the failure/prefix function of the needle and scan the haystack once without moving backwards
compare a rolling polynomial hash of each window with the needle's hash and verify on a hash match
compute the Z-array of needle + separator + haystack and report the first position whose Z-value equals the needle length
compare from the right end of the window and shift by a bad-character table built from the needle
delegate to Python's built-in substring search: str.find, str.index or the in operator

T04.spec_text:
Task: write a Python function solve(haystack, needle) that returns the index of the first position at which the string needle occurs as a contiguous substring of the string haystack, or -1 if needle is not a substring of haystack. Both strings consist only of lowercase English letters, with 1 <= len(haystack) <= 2000 and 1 <= len(needle) <= 200. Indices start at 0. If needle is longer than haystack, the answer is -1.

Use only the Python standard library. Return only one ```python code block containing the function solve and any helpers, with no example usage and no explanation.

catalogue.display_name: a hash set of seen values
catalogue.mechanism: scan once and remember seen values in a set (or a boolean/count array) until one repeats
sort a copy of the list and return the first value equal to its neighbour
treat i -> nums[i] as a linked list and run tortoise-and-hare to find the cycle entrance

catalogue.display_name: binary search on the value range
catalogue.mechanism: binary-search the value range, counting how many elements are at most mid (pigeonhole)

catalogue.display_name: index marking in the input array
catalogue.mechanism: mark visited values inside the list itself by negating or swapping entries at index value

T06.spec_text:
Task: write a Python function solve(nums) that returns the repeated value in nums. The argument nums is a list of n + 1 integers, where 1 <= n <= 10000, and every value lies between 1 and n inclusive. Exactly one value occurs more than once, and it may occur two or more times; every other value occurs at most once. Return the repeated value as an int.

Use only the Python standard library. Return only one ```python code block containing the function solve and any helpers, with no example usage and no explanation.

catalogue.display_name: a hash map of seen values
catalogue.mechanism: scan once, storing each value's index in a dict and looking up target minus the current value
sort (value, index) pairs and move two pointers inwards from both ends
check every pair i < j with two nested loops
sort (value, index) pairs and binary-search the complement of each value

T05.spec_text:
Task: write a Python function solve(nums, target) that returns a list [i, j] of two indices with i < j such that nums[i] + nums[j] == target. The argument nums is a list of integers with 2 <= len(nums) <= 2000 and every value between -10**9 and 10**9 inclusive; target is an integer. Each input has exactly one pair of indices whose values add up to target, so the answer is unique. The two indices must be different positions, although the values at them may be equal.

Use only the Python standard library. Return only one ```python code block containing the function solve and any helpers, with no example usage and no explanation.

catalogue.mechanism: start a breadth-first traversal with a FIFO queue from every unvisited node and count the starts
start a depth-first traversal (recursion or an explicit LIFO stack) from every unvisited node and count the starts
union the endpoints of every edge in a disjoint-set forest and count the roots
give every node its own label and repeatedly sweep the edges, lowering labels to the neighbour minimum until nothing changes

T10.spec_text:
Task: write a Python function solve(n, edges) that returns the number of connected components of an undirected graph. The nodes are the integers 0 to n - 1, with 1 <= n <= 300. The argument edges is a list of pairs [u, v] with 0 <= u, v < n and u != v, each joining nodes u and v; 0 <= len(edges) <= 1500 and no pair of nodes is joined twice. A node with no edges forms a component on its own.

Use only the Python standard library. Return only one ```python code block containing the function solve and any helpers, with no example usage and no explanation.

catalogue.mechanism: sort by end (or by start keeping the smaller end) and greedily keep every interval that starts after the last kept end
sort by end; dp over prefixes where keeping interval i jumps to the last compatible interval found by binary search
recursive take-or-skip choice over intervals sorted by start, memoised on the index

catalogue.display_name: a longest path in the interval graph
catalogue.mechanism: build the compatibility DAG (i -> j when i ends before j starts) and take its longest path by DP over all pairs

R1.spec_text:
Task: write a Python function solve(intervals) that returns the minimum number of intervals that have to be removed so that no two of the remaining intervals overlap. The argument intervals is a list of pairs [start, end] of integers with start < end, 1 <= len(intervals) <= 1000 and every value between -50000 and 50000 inclusive. Two intervals that only touch, such as [1, 2] and [2, 3], count as non-overlapping. Return the count as an int.

Use only the Python standard library. Return only one ```python code block containing the function solve and any helpers, with no example usage and no explanation.

catalogue.mechanism: loop from the bottom up, keeping the last two values (or a table)
recurse on F(n-1) + F(n-2) with a cache (dict or functools.lru_cache/cache)
raise the 2x2 matrix [[1,1],[1,0]] to the n-th power by repeated squaring
use F(2k) = F(k)(2F(k+1) - F(k)) and F(2k+1) = F(k)^2 + F(k+1)^2 over the bits of n

T08.spec_text:
Task: write a Python function solve(n) that returns the n-th Fibonacci number as an exact Python int. The sequence is defined by F(0) = 0, F(1) = 1 and F(n) = F(n - 1) + F(n - 2) for n >= 2, so F(10) = 55. The argument n is an integer with 0 <= n <= 500, and the result must be exact for every n in that range.

Use only the Python standard library. Return only one ```python code block containing the function solve and any helpers, with no example usage and no explanation.

catalogue.mechanism: compute in-degrees and repeatedly pop zero in-degree nodes from a queue, decrementing their successors
depth-first search with three colours; emit nodes in post-order and reverse, reporting a back edge as a cycle
repeatedly rescan the remaining nodes for one with no remaining prerequisite and delete it, without a maintained queue
assign each node its longest-path depth from the sources and output nodes sorted by depth

R3.spec_text:
Task: write a Python function solve(n, prerequisites) that orders n tasks numbered 0 to n - 1. Each pair [a, b] in the list prerequisites means that task b has to come before task a. Return a list that contains every task exactly once and respects every pair; if several orders are valid, any of them is accepted. If no valid order exists, return an empty list. Here 1 <= n <= 500, 0 <= len(prerequisites) <= 2000, a != b, and no pair is repeated.

Use only the Python standard library. Return only one ```python code block containing the function solve and any helpers, with no example usage and no explanation.

catalogue.mechanism: sort by start and sweep once, extending the last merged interval or starting a new one
insert intervals into a tree of nodes keyed by start with a max-end field and merge through overlap queries
union every pair of overlapping intervals in a disjoint-set forest and take min start / max end per root

T13.spec_text:
Task: write a Python function solve(intervals) that merges overlapping intervals. The argument intervals is a list of pairs [start, end] of integers with 0 <= start <= end <= 10000 and 1 <= len(intervals) <= 1500, given in no particular order. Two intervals belong to the same merged interval when they overlap or touch, for example [1, 3] and [3, 5] merge into [1, 5]. Return the merged intervals as a list of [start, end] lists sorted by start, with no two of them overlapping or touching.

Use only the Python standard library. Return only one ```python code block containing the function solve and any helpers, with no example usage and no explanation.

catalogue.mechanism: hand-written lower/upper-bound binary searches (loops or recursion) over the index range
bisect.bisect_left and bisect.bisect_right from the standard library
double a bound (1, 2, 4, ...) until it passes the target, then binary-search inside the bracket

R6.spec_text:
Task: write a Python function solve(nums, target) that returns a list [first, last] holding the first and the last index at which target occurs in nums, or [-1, -1] if target does not occur. The argument nums is a list of integers sorted in non-decreasing order, with 0 <= len(nums) <= 100000 and every value between -10**9 and 10**9 inclusive; target is an integer in the same range.

Use only the Python standard library. Return only one ```python code block containing the function solve and any helpers, with no example usage and no explanation.

catalogue.mechanism: count the values and sort the distinct values by count (or Counter.most_common() with no argument)
count the values and keep the k best in a heap (heapq push/pop of size k, heapq.nlargest or Counter.most_common(k))
count the values, put each value into bucket[count] for counts 0..n and read buckets from the highest
count the values and partition the distinct values by count around a pivot until the top k are separated

T14.spec_text:
Task: write a Python function solve(nums, k) that returns the k values that occur most often in nums, as a list in any order. The argument nums is a list of integers with 1 <= len(nums) <= 10000 and every value between -10000 and 10000 inclusive; k is an integer between 1 and the number of distinct values in nums. The inputs are chosen so that the answer is unique: the k-th and (k+1)-th highest frequencies always differ.

Use only the Python standard library. Return only one ```python code block containing the function solve and any helpers, with no example usage and no explanation.

catalogue.mechanism: dp[i] = 1 + max dp[j] over earlier j with nums[j] < nums[i], comparing all pairs
keep a tails array of the smallest tail per length and binary-search (bisect) where each value goes

catalogue.display_name: a Fenwick tree over compressed values
catalogue.mechanism: compress values to ranks and query/update prefix maxima in a Fenwick (or segment) tree

T11.spec_text:
Task: write a Python function solve(nums) that returns the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence of nums. A subsequence keeps the original order of the chosen elements but need not be contiguous, and strictly increasing means each chosen value is larger than the one before it. The argument nums is a list of integers with 1 <= len(nums) <= 1000 and every value between -10000 and 10000 inclusive.

Use only the Python standard library. Return only one ```python code block containing the function solve and any helpers, with no example usage and no explanation.

        return []
    
    # Separate starts and ends
    starts = []
    ends = []
    for interval in intervals:
        starts.append(interval[0])
        ends.append(interval[1])

    starts.sort()
    ends.sort()
    
    merged = []
    current_start = starts[0]

        if starts[i] <= current_end:
            # Overlapping or touching, merge
            current_end = max(current_end, ends[i])
        else:
            # No overlap, add current interval
            merged.append([current_start, current_end])
            current_start = starts[i]
            current_end = ends[i]
    
    # Add the last interval
    merged.append([current_start, current_end])

    current_end = min_start - 1

        # Check if the point is the start of any interval
